title: Euclid's First Major Data Release Includes 900 Million Galaxies
byline: Elias Reed Published: Nov 13 2026, 8:49 AM EST
excerpt: ESA and the Euclid Consortium released 1.7 petabytes of data from 13 months of observations, including more than 900 million galaxies.
content:
The European Space Agency and the Euclid Consortium have released the mission's first major collection of science data. The November 12 release, called DR1-Foundation, covers roughly 13 months of observations and contains about 1.7 petabytes of data. It includes information on more than 900 million galaxies, according to ESA.

The release also includes around 15,000 strong gravitational-lensing candidates, more than 60 million quasar candidates and spectra from over 160 million sources. These measurements give astronomers a broad dataset to search, compare and analyze. The Euclid Consortium says the released area covers about 1,900 square degrees, including deep-field observations.

Euclid is designed to map the large-scale structure of the universe over a six-year mission. Its observations will help scientists study how galaxies are distributed and investigate dark matter and dark energy. The new release provides tools for that work, but it does not announce a new measurement that resolves what those components are.

What the numbers mean

The 900-million figure describes objects catalogued across the released data, not 900 million galaxies newly discovered from scratch. Some are known objects now measured in a uniform survey; others may be new or better characterized. Strong-lensing candidates are also candidates requiring follow-up and confirmation, not all confirmed lenses.

Gravitational lensing occurs when a foreground galaxy's gravity bends light from a more distant object. These distortions can help scientists study the mass of galaxies and clusters, including matter that does not emit light. A larger set of candidates increases the opportunities for research, but each object's properties still need analysis.

The Reuters report describes the release as a milestone for the mission. The definitive value will depend on what astronomers find when they use the dataset, and those results will emerge over time.

A first step, not the final map

ESA says the full Data Release 1 is scheduled for 2027 and will add further data products. Euclid's final survey is expected to cover a much larger area of sky. Researchers will use the current release to test methods, identify unusual objects and refine measurements before later releases broaden the picture.

For the public, the important news is the scale and accessibility of the data. Astronomers outside the mission team can work with the material, increasing the chance of independent analysis. The release is a research resource, not a finished explanation of the dark universe.

Why open data can speed discovery

A large mission dataset is useful not only for the scientists who designed the observations. Public release allows independent researchers to test new measurement methods, search for unusual objects and compare Euclid's catalogues with other surveys. It can also enable work that the original team did not anticipate. Data access is one reason the release is a major milestone, even before it produces a headline-grabbing new conclusion about the universe.

The catalogue is not a final census of everything in the observed sky. Detecting faint objects, separating overlapping sources and confirming lens candidates all require careful analysis. The survey will also expand as Euclid collects more observations. The current release should therefore be presented as a substantial first resource and a foundation for later data, rather than the completed three-dimensional map promised at the end of the mission.

What astronomers can study in the release

The European Space Agency's Euclid mission is designed to chart the distribution of galaxies and the large-scale structure of the universe. The telescope observes in visible and near-infrared light and measures the shapes, distances and spectra of cosmic objects. Its long-term goal is to help researchers study dark matter and dark energy by showing how galaxies and galaxy clusters are distributed across space and how that distribution changes over cosmic time.

The November 12 DR1-Foundation release covers about 1,900 square degrees, around 14 percent of the area planned for Euclid's six-year survey. In addition to more than 900 million galaxies, it includes around 15,000 strong-lensing candidates, over 60 million quasar candidates and spectra from more than 160 million sources. ESA's release overviewdescribes the catalogue and the data products. Strong gravitational lenses occur when the gravity of a closer object bends light from a more distant source, sometimes producing arcs or rings.

Those counts are not all new discoveries. Some catalogued galaxies were already known; Euclid's contribution is to observe and characterize a very large sample consistently across its survey. The lens figures are candidates, which still need expert review and follow-up. A large catalogue improves the odds of finding rare objects, but it does not make every entry equally certain.

Why releasing data is news

A public data release lets researchers beyond the mission team examine the observations. They can test new analysis methods, search for unusual objects and compare Euclid's measurements with data from other telescopes. The Euclid Consortium says it combined machine learning, citizen science and expert validation to identify candidate lenses, illustrating how different methods can help sort enormous datasets.

The release is a foundation, not the completed three-dimensional map. ESA plans a fuller Data Release 1 in 2027, with additional measurements needed for studies of galaxy shapes and the cosmic web. Euclid will also continue collecting observations. The current dataset establishes a major first base for research, while later releases will expand the area and add products.

The science questions remain open. Dark matter is inferred from its gravitational effects, while dark energy describes the observed acceleration of cosmic expansion. Euclid data can help test models of both, but no single catalogue can reveal their physical nature on its own. Researchers must combine the survey with theory, independent observations and careful treatment of measurement uncertainty.

The headline should therefore focus on the scale and accessibility of the release, rather than imply that Euclid has solved the dark universe. The milestone is that scientists can now work with a substantial, shared survey dataset and use it to pursue many lines of research.

What the next Euclid releases should add

The DR1-Foundation release is an initial major batch, and ESA has scheduled a fuller Data Release 1 for 2027. Later data should cover more of the planned survey and include additional measurements useful for studying galaxy shapes and the distribution of matter. Those additions matter because astronomers need more than a list of objects to build a three-dimensional picture: they need reliable distances, shape measurements and information about how galaxies cluster. The timeline is subject to mission operations, and the current data are already available for analysis. The main point is that this release begins a longer sequence of public scientific resources.

The release also contains data about stars in the Milky Way bulge from a separate Euclid survey component, while the main story focuses on distant galaxies and the large-scale universe. Keeping those pieces distinct helps readers understand that a single mission can support several areas of astronomy. For this article, the strongest focus remains the 900-million-galaxy dataset and the lens candidates. A separate story could explore the stellar survey, but it should not mix all mission results into one claim about dark matter.

Key Questions Answered

How much data did Euclid release?

About 1.7 petabytes from roughly 13 months of observations.

Has Euclid solved dark matter or dark energy?

No. The dataset is intended to support research into the universe's structure and these open questions.

Are all 15,000 lens candidates confirmed discoveries?

No. They are candidates identified in the release and require follow-up or expert confirmation; the catalogue also includes previously known objects.
